content: Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is a severe form of tuberculosis that affects the central nervous system, often leading to high rates of mortality and long-term disability. International guidelines generally recommend longer antituberculous treatment (ATT) regimens for TBM compared to pulmonary tuberculosis to reduce the risk of relapse. However, prolonged treatment regimens are associated with challenges such as poor adherence, which can lead to increased relapse rates, the emergence of drug resistance, and higher costs for both patients and healthcare systems. The objective of this study was to compare the effects of short-course (six months) ATT regimens with prolonged-course regimens in individuals with TBM. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted up to March 31, 2016, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, INDMED, and the South Asian Database of Controlled Clinical Trials. Ongoing trials were identified through the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP) and ClinicalTrials.gov. Reference lists of articles were reviewed, and researchers in the field were contacted for additional information. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and prospective cohort studies involving adults and children with TBM who were treated with ATT regimens containing rifampicin for at least six months. The primary outcome of interest was relapse, and studies were required to have a minimum follow-up period of six months after treatment completion. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. When necessary, study authors were contacted for additional information. Most of the data came from single-arm cohort studies without direct comparisons between shortand prolonged-course regimens. Findings were pooled and analyzed separately for each group of cohorts. A total of 18 studies, including four RCTs, 13 prospective cohort studies, and one unpublished ongoing cohort study, met the inclusion criteria. These studies involved 2098 participants with TBM. None of the RCTs directly compared six-month regimens with longer regimens, so the data were analyzed as individual cohorts to determine relapse rates. The analysis included 20 cohorts reported in 18 studies, with 19 cohorts included in the main analysis. Seven cohorts (458 participants) were treated for six months, while 12 cohorts (1423 participants) were treated for longer durations (ranging from eight to 16 months). The unpublished ongoing cohort study from India included 217 participants. The cohorts treated for six months had a higher proportion of participants with stage III (severe) disease (33.2% vs. 16.9%), while the cohorts treated for longer durations had a higher proportion of participants with concurrent HIV infection (0/458 vs. 122/1423). Despite variations in treatment regimens, most cohorts received isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide during the intensive phase. Follow-up beyond 18 months after treatment completion was achieved in three of the seven six-month cohorts and five of the 12 longer-duration cohorts. All studies had potential sources of bias in estimating relapse rates, and comparisons between cohorts were likely confounded. Relapse was a rare event in both groups, occurring in 0.8% of participants treated for six months (3/369) and 0.8% of those treated for longer durations (7/915). Only one death due to relapse was reported in each group. However, the overall mortality rate was higher in the cohorts treated for longer than six months (31.4%, 447/1423) compared to those treated for six months (12.7%, 58/458). Most deaths occurred during the first six months of treatment in both groups, suggesting that the difference in mortality rates was not directly related to the duration of ATT but rather to confounding factors. Clinical cure rates were higher in the six-month treatment group (89.1%, 408/458) compared to the longer treatment group (73.7%, 984/1336), consistent with the observed differences in mortality. Treatment default rates were low in both groups, with 1.1% (4/370) in the six-month group and 2.3% (8/355) in the longer treatment group. Adherence to treatment was not well-reported in the studies. In conclusion, most deaths occurred within the first six months of treatment, and relapse was uncommon regardless of the treatment regimen. However, these findings are based on observational data, and the potential for confounding limits the ability to draw definitive conclusions. Additionally, the data primarily involved HIV-negative participants, so the results may not be applicable to HIV-positive individuals. Well-designed RCTs or large prospective cohort studies with long follow-up periods are needed to address the uncertainty regarding the safety and efficacy of six-month ATT regimens for TBM.
